identification.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks Storm-2657 as a financially motivated actor that compromises employee accounts, reaches HR software-as-a-service platforms (primarily Workday), and redirects salary payments to attacker-controlled bank accounts. Microsoft calls the technique 'payroll pirate' attacks [S1]. Press coverage says Microsoft observed phishing against US university employees since March 2025 [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: phishing activity since March 2025, with the Workday-focused campaign observed in the first half of 2025; the report was published 2025-10-09 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-2657 (a developing-cluster designation). Microsoft calls the technique 'payroll pirate' attacks [S1].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is stated. Microsoft describes Storm-2657 as financially motivated [S1]. The post makes no statement about the actor's country of origin [S1].
attribution.confidence: No confidence level is stated in Microsoft's report [S1].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry on compromised accounts, phishing messages, inbox rules and Workday audit events, with collaboration from Workday [S1].

objectives: Direct financial gain by diverting employee salary payments to attacker-controlled bank accounts [S1]. Microsoft says the technique could apply to any SaaS system holding HR, payroll or bank data [S1].

targeting.notes: Microsoft counted 11 successfully compromised accounts at three universities, which sent phishing to nearly 6,000 accounts at 25 universities [S1]. Microsoft says US-based organizations, particularly higher education, are targeted, and that no Workday product vulnerability is involved [S1].

capabilities.summary: Social engineering with adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing to capture credentials and MFA codes; some victim accounts lacked MFA [S1]. Lures included illness-exposure notices, faculty-misconduct notices and institution-tailored compensation and benefits updates, some using Google Docs links that redirect to attacker domains [S1]. After access to Exchange Online, the actor created inbox rules (some named with only special characters) to hide Workday payroll-change notifications, enrolled its own phone numbers as MFA devices via Workday profiles or Duo settings, used SSO to reach Workday, and changed payroll and bank details. Compromised accounts were reused to phish colleagues and other universities [S1]. No malware, exploits or published IOCs are described [S1].

campaigns.name: University phishing wave begins
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports phishing activity against US university employees since March 2025, with the Workday-focused campaign observed in the first half of 2025 [S1].

campaigns.name: Example inbox-rule and payroll-change event
campaigns.summary: Microsoft cites an audit sequence of inbox rule creation followed by Workday payroll changes on 14 August 2025 as an example of the pattern [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft public disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft publishes its investigation: 11 compromised accounts at three universities, phishing to nearly 6,000 accounts at 25 universities, hunting queries, and mitigation advice including phishing-resistant MFA [S1][S2].

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated actor tracked by Microsoft as Storm-2657; origin not stated [S1].
diamond.capability: AiTM phishing for credentials and MFA codes, inbox rules to hide alerts, attacker-enrolled MFA devices, SSO access to Workday, payroll and bank detail changes [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Attacker domains reached through phishing links, including redirects from Google Docs links; Microsoft refers to malicious domain indicators but the post text contains no published domains [S1].
diamond.victim: US university employees with Exchange Online and Workday accounts; 11 compromised accounts at three universities in Microsoft's count [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financial crime with no stated political motive [S1].
diamond.technology: Exchange Online, Workday, SSO, and Duo or Workday MFA enrollment; weakness is missing or non-phishing-resistant MFA, not a Workday vulnerability [S1].

gaps: Actor origin, size and infrastructure are not stated by Microsoft [S1].
No confidence level and no published IOCs (domains, IPs, phone numbers) in the Microsoft post as retrieved [S1].
Number of victims whose pay was actually diverted, and total losses, are not given [S1].
No US government (FBI/IC3/CISA) advisory, indictment or other vendor cluster report on this actor was found; government sites were not accessible.
Press articles (The Register, BleepingComputer, TechRadar) were seen as search summaries only.
A claimed related cluster (Storm-2755, Canada) could not be confirmed by search and was removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the identity and HR-SaaS layer (Exchange Online mailboxes, SSO, Workday, MFA enrollment) of civilian-education and similar organizations, not military networks [S1]. STEP 2: The actor is financially motivated and uses no malware or exploits; the main enabler is missing or phishable MFA [S1]. STEP 3: Template is AiTM phish, mailbox access, hidden-notification inbox rule, attacker MFA device, SSO to Workday, bank detail change, then internal and cross-institution phishing [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued payroll diversion against universities and other HR-SaaS-using employers. MDCOA is the same chain aimed at DoD civilians, contractors or military-affiliated universities and academic partners, producing financial loss and account-takeover footholds in mail tenants. Candidate indicators: inbox rules with special-character names or rules deleting Workday mail, 'Add iOS Device' or 'Add Android Device' Workday events, 'Change My Account' or 'Manage Payment Elections' events, new MFA methods after risky sign-ins, and bulk email from .edu senders [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: threat is low-sophistication but high-volume against identity systems; track via mailbox-rule and MFA-change telemetry rather than network indicators [S1]. (2) Authorities: remediation is an owner-operator action (password reset, session revocation, MFA device review, payroll reversal) and involves HR and finance offices, not only cyber staff [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: enforce phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2, Windows Hello, passkeys) for personnel systems and privileged roles first [S1]. (4) Coordination: involve the SaaS vendor (Microsoft credited Workday collaboration), HR/finance, and law enforcement channels for fraud recovery; academic partners should be warned of cross-institution phishing [S1].
